Here is the thing that confuses people who did not grow up here. When an American asks how you are doing, it is not a question. It is a doorbell. You are not supposed to answer it with information. You say good, how are you, and then the actual conversation can start, or not. People hear that and decide that Americans are fake. I would argue the opposite. The small talk is not the conversation. It is the part that makes the conversation possible, and we are honestly terrible at getting there without it. If you skipped it, you would be the person who walks into a room and starts talking about interest rates. And here is what nobody tells visitors. The easiest opener in this country is not a question about the person. It is a comment about the room. The line, the weather, the thing on the table between you. If I wanted to talk to a stranger in an airport, I would not ask them where they are from. I would say something about the gate, and then wait.

I have been behind this bar for eleven years, and you get good at reading which people are going to talk to each other. It is never the loud ones. It is the person who takes off their coat slowly and looks around first. Here is what I have learned. Nobody starts a conversation because they are brave. They start it because somebody gave them a reason. So I put a bowl of something on the bar, right between two people who came in alone, and I walk away. Nine times out of ten they are talking in four minutes. If I stood there and introduced them, it would die in thirty seconds. Everybody hates being introduced. What people want is an excuse, and the excuse can be anything. A dog. A bad song on the speaker. The fact that the kitchen closed. If I gave you one piece of advice for traveling alone, it would be this. Sit at the bar, not at a table. A table is a door with a lock on it.
